extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/olympiad students learning real analysis and p-adic numbers
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter explaining limits, infinite series, p-adic numbers, and basic differentiation with definitions, propositions, and worked examples geared to contest/undergraduate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of an infinite series (Definition 26.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A series ∑ a_k converges to a limit L if the sequence of partial sums s_n = a1 + ··· + a_n converges to L. Otherwise it diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces questions about 'adding infinitely many numbers' to limits of sequences (partial sums). Examples: use partial sums to compute telescoping sums and to test divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation for divergence to +∞ for nonnegative terms (Abuse 26.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If all a_k ≥ 0 and the partial sums are unbounded, it is customary to write ∑ a_k = ∞ to denote divergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a conventional shorthand used throughout; it is tied to the monotonicity of partial sums when terms are nonnegative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: infinite sum as limit of partial sums
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'infinite sum' is actually the limit of its partial sums; there is no literal infinite addition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows sequences of rational numbers to converge to irrational sums; distinguishes ordinary convergent series from summation-by-definition conventions (e.g., analytic continuations assigning values to divergent formal sums).

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescoping-series technique (Example 26.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute k-th partial sum by expressing general term as a telescoping difference so most terms cancel; then take limit of partial sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ∑_{k=1}^∞ 1/[k(k+1)] has k-th partial sum = 1 − 1/(n+1) → 1. Useful pattern to recognize in manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping/comparison proof of harmonic series divergence (Example 26.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show divergence by lower-bounding partial sums via grouping (e.g., group terms between powers of two) to deduce partial sums grow without bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provided proof bounds 2^n partial sum ≥ 1 + (n−1)/2, hence unbounded. Use grouping/lower bounds for monotone nonnegative series to show divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonnegative series: bounded partial sums iff convergence (Proposition 26.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a series ∑ a_k with a_k ≥ 0, the series converges if and only if the sequence of partial sums is bounded (i.e., there exists M with s_n < M for all n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses monotonicity s1 ≤ s2 ≤ ··· and supremum; equivalent to the completeness/Cauchy arguments. This justifies writing ∑ a_k < ∞ as shorthand for convergence for nonnegative terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorthand ∑ a_k < ∞ for nonnegative convergent series (Abuse 26.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonnegative a_k, it is customary to write ∑ a_k < ∞ as shorthand meaning the series converges to a finite limit (or equivalently the partial sums are bounded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a notational convenience used in later arguments and problem statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute convergence (Definition 26.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A series ∑ a_k is absolutely convergent if ∑ |a_k| converges; if ∑ a_k converges but ∑ |a_k| does not, it is conditionally convergent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute convergence is a stronger notion with better rearrangement properties; many convergence tests (comparison, ratio) are applied to |a_k|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute convergence implies convergence (Proposition 26.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∑ |a_k| converges, then ∑ a_k also converges (in the usual sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard proof uses Cauchy criterion: partial sums of |a_k| being Cauchy implies partial sums of a_k are Cauchy. This is the basis for many standard convergence arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutations preserve sum for absolutely convergent series (Theorem 26.5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∑ a_k is absolutely convergent with sum L, then any permutation (rearrangement) of its terms also converges to L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses tail control from absolute convergence and finite rearrangement of initial segment; ensures rearrangements do not change limit when absolute convergence holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonnegative series can be rearranged freely
rubrics_metrics.description: When all terms are nonnegative, rearrangement of terms does not affect convergence or the sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from monotonicity of partial sums for nonnegative terms; often noted as practical comfort since many series in applications are nonnegative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann rearrangement theorem (Theorem 26.5.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∑ a_k converges conditionally (converges but not absolutely), then by permuting the terms one can obtain a series that converges to any prescribed real number (or diverges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows rearrangements are 'as bad as possible' for conditionally convergent series; warns not to rearrange conditionally convergent series unless justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of a function at a point (ε–δ definition, Definition 26.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f: R→R and p in domain, L is lim_{x→p} f(x) if for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that 0<|x−p|<δ implies |f(x)−L|<ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crucial note: the definition requires x ≠ p, so the limit does not depend on f(p). Use this to reason about removable/essential discontinuities; examples illustrate 'hole' functions where f(p) is arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity as equality of limit and value
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f is continuous at p iff lim_{x→p} f(x) exists and equals f(p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise given to show equivalence; examples: piecewise rational function and sin(x)/x at 0 showing limit behavior independent of assigned value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit at infinity (Definition 26.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: lim_{x→∞} f(x) = L means: for every ε>0 there exists M such that if x > M then |f(x)−L|<ε (similarly for −∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the usual epsilon–M formulation for limits at infinity; examples: lim_{x→∞} 1/x = 0 with explicit M = 1/ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison test for absolute convergence (Problem 26C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∑ b_n is absolutely convergent and |a_n| ≤ |b_n| for all n, then ∑ a_n is absolutely convergent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic comparison test; used to deduce absolute convergence from a dominating absolutely convergent series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric series test and sum (Problem 26D / Prop 27.3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For real r with |r|<1, 1 + r + r^2 + ··· converges absolutely; more generally in p-adics, if |x|_p < 1 then 1 + x + x^2 + ··· = 1/(1−x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides both real and p-adic versions; in p-adics convergence follows from |x^n|_p → 0, and partial-sum formula 1−x^{n+1} over 1−x tends to 1/(1−x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating series test (Leibniz test, Problem 26E)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a_0 ≥ a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ 0 and lim_{n→∞} a_n = 0, then ∑ (-1)^n a_n converges (may be conditionally convergent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard alternating series criterion; gives convergence without absolute convergence. Use monotone decreasing and vanishing terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of p-adic integers Z_p (Definition 27.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A p-adic integer is a compatible sequence (x_1 mod p, x_2 mod p^2, x_3 mod p^3, …) with x_i ≡ x_j (mod p^i) for i<j. The set Z_p forms a ring under componentwise operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inverse-limit definition formalizes keeping all residue information modulo p^e simultaneously; examples illustrate integers embedding into Z_p and nonstandard p-adic integers (e.g., 1 + p + p^2 + …).

rubrics_metrics.name: Base-p expansion viewpoint of Z_p (27.2.ii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of Z_p can be written as 'base p' expansions x = ∑_{k≥0} a_k p^k = … a_2 a_1 a_0 (digits a_k ∈ {0,…,p−1}), infinite to the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives intuition similar to formal power series; negative integers also have infinite base-p expansions. Useful mental model: p-adic integers as 'possibly infinite base-p expansions' or 'Taylor series with base p.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-multiples of p are invertible in Z_p (Proposition 27.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: An element x ∈ Z_p is invertible iff its residue modulo p is nonzero (x_1 ≠ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to invertibility of power series with nonzero constant term. Demonstrated by constructing inverses modulo p^e inductively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Q_p and multiplicative decomposition (Definition 27.2.8 / Proposition 27.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Q_p is the field of fractions of Z_p. Every nonzero element of Q_p can be written uniquely as p^k · u with k ∈ Z and u ∈ Z_p^×; equivalently as a (formal) Laurent-series-style base-p expansion with finitely many negative powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: Z_p ↔ K[[X]], Q_p ↔ K((X)). In practice denominators needed are only powers of p; do not think of arbitrary x/y with x,y∈Z_p for intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: p-adic valuation and absolute value (Definition 27.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ν_p(x) as exponent of p in x (largest e with x ≡ 0 mod p^e for x∈Z_p or the unique k in decomposition p^k u). Set |x|_p = p^{−ν_p(x)}, with |0|_p = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metric captures 'closeness' in terms of high-power p-agreement; large ν_p(x−y) (hence small |x−y|_p) means x and y agree modulo high p^e.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultrametric (strong triangle) inequality (Proposition 27.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any x,y ∈ Z_p, |x + y|_p ≤ max(|x|_p, |y|_p). Equality holds if |x|_p ≠ |y|_p (but not only in that case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stronger-than-usual triangle inequality leads to many nonintuitive p-adic topological properties (e.g., every triangle is isosceles in a metric sense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence in Q_p and series convergence criterion (Definition 27.3.4 / Proposition 27.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequence s_n converges to L in Q_p iff |s_n − L|_p → 0. A series ∑ x_k converges in Q_p iff the sequence of partial sums converges; equivalently (Proposition 27.3.5) ∑ x_k converges iff |x_k|_p → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Q_p, the necessary condition |x_k|_p → 0 is also sufficient for series convergence (contrast with real analysis). Proof leverages ultrametric properties and stabilization of residues modulo p^e.

rubrics_metrics.name: p-adic geometric series (Proposition 27.3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x ∈ Z_p with |x|_p < 1, then 1 + x + x^2 + ··· converges to 1/(1 − x) in Q_p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mirrors real-case algebraic identity; convergence follows since x^n → 0 in p-adic norm. Example: 1 + 3 + 3^2 + … = −1/2 in Z_3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of Q_p (Theorem 27.3.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Q_p is the completion of Q with respect to the p-adic absolute value |·|_p; equivalently, Q_p is complete under the p-adic metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the justification for working in Q_p rather than Q when doing p-adic analysis, analogous to working in R for real analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mahler expansion: continuous functions Z_p → Q_p (Theorem 27.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any continuous f: Z_p → Q_p can be written uniquely as f(x) = ∑_{n≥0} a_n (x choose n), with lim_{n→∞} a_n = 0, where a_n = ∑_{k=0}^n (n choose k)(−1)^{n−k} f(k). Conversely any sequence a_n→0 defines a continuous function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The coefficients a_n are Mahler coefficients (finite-difference expressions). This provides a complete description of continuous p-adic functions and connects with finite-difference methods used in contest math.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyticity criterion via Mahler coefficients (Theorem 27.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Mahler series f(x)=∑ a_n (x choose n) is analytic on Z_p (i.e., equals a convergent power series ∑ c_n x^n on Z_p) iff lim_{n→∞} a_n / n! = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a practical criterion distinguishing continuous functions from analytic ones in the p-adic sense; used to prove finiteness results about zeros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strassmann's theorem (Theorem 27.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f: Z_p → Q_p is analytic, then f has finitely many zeros in Z_p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful finiteness statement used in applications (e.g., Skolem-Mahler-Lech). It is an analog of results about zeros of analytic functions over non-Archimedean fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skolem-Mahler-Lech theorem (Theorem 27.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an integral linear recurrence (x_n) satisfying x_n = c_1 x_{n−1} + ··· + c_k x_{n−k} with integer coefficients, the set of indices {i | x_i = 0} is eventually periodic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch uses p-adic methods: pick prime p not dividing det A, use Mahler expansion and Strassmann to extend index-sequence to Z_p and conclude finite/frequency structure of zeros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of derivative (Definition 28.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f: U→R with U open and p∈U, f is differentiable at p if lim_{h→0} [f(p+h) − f(p)] / h exists; the limit is f'(p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivative is defined on open sets because h→0 requires points on both sides. Convention: treat f' as a function, and differentiability implies continuity (exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiability implies continuity (Exercise 28.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is differentiable at p then f is continuous at p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard elementary consequence of the definition of derivative; included as an exercise to confirm understanding of limit definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic differentiation rules (Theorem 28.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sum rule: (f+g)' = f' + g'. Product rule: (f·g)' = f' g + f g'. Chain rule: (g◦f)' = g'(f(x)) · f'(x) when compositions are defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard calculus differentiation rules; proofs given (or left trivial) using the limit definitions. These are essential computational tools for differentiable functions on open intervals.
